classification_signals: Abstract states 'This study describes the conflicting perceptions... explored by extracting criticism and comment from literature... case study of the Igualada Cemetery is used to describe...'

Methodology section (page 9) states 'This study is a descriptive practicum with some prescriptive conclusions. It describes the relationship between the fundamental subjects of weathering and perception... A literature review was the means of identifying the salient points... The main thrust was to find evidence of the perceptions of weathering, as read in the criticism of others.'
Direction of the Study (page 16) states 'The primary example of weathering in cemetery design is the analysis of Igualada Cemetery.'
title: The Dichotomy of Weathering in the Cemetery: An Investigation of Experiences and Expressions in Landscape Architecture

findings.consequent: influence on landscapes
findings.quote: The process of weathering always influences landscapes.

findings.consequent: perceptions
findings.quote: perceptions of the effects of weathering may be varied and profound.

findings.antecedent: relationship between people and landscapes (human built and natural)
findings.consequent: psychological event
findings.quote: The relationship between people and landscapes (both human built and natural) is a complex psychological event.

findings.consequent: conflicting perceptions (bereaved vs. bystanders)
findings.quote: The study describes the conflicting perceptions of weathered forms in the cemetery from the perspective of two groups.

findings.antecedent: Igualada Cemetery design (intentional allowance of weathering)
findings.consequent: expressive place for all visitors
findings.quote: At Igualada, the cemetery is designed as an expressive place for all visitors and the process of weathering is an integral part of that expression.

findings.antecedent: process of weathering in the cemetery
findings.consequent: positive aspects
findings.quote: The investigation uncovers a number of positive aspects of the process of weathering in the cemetery.

findings.consequent: physical and psychological qualities of materials
findings.quote: Weathering affects both the physical and psychological qualities of these same materials, as any viewer perceives them.

findings.consequent: different perceptions of material transformations
findings.quote: weathering affects many different perceptions of such transformations of materials.

findings.consequent: relationship between people and material objects of the environment
findings.quote: Materiality is the relationship between people and the material objects of the environment.

findings.consequent: rich, expressive places in urban environment
findings.quote: By clarifying the subject of the cemetery as a place of conflicting perceptions, landscape architects can develop designs that utilize a keen understanding of weathering, material characteristics and public views. This can lead to rich, expressive places in our urban environment, if the process of weathering is found to have positive aesthetic merit.

findings.consequent: symbolic and narrative qualities that make landscapes rich in meaning and interpretations
findings.quote: Weathering can have many different physical manifestations. Also, it can have symbolic and narrative qualities that make landscapes into places rich in meaning and possible interpretations.

findings.antecedent: weathering (as an expressive part of cemetery design)
findings.consequent: demonstration of abstract ideas (life, death, mortality, nature)
findings.quote: the process and results of weathering can be an expressive part of a cemetery design, demonstrating abstract ideas such as life, death, mortality and nature.

findings.consequent: cue of time and change in outdoor places
findings.quote: Because weathering is found in all outdoor places, it is a cue of time and change.

findings.consequent: complimentary effects on landscape forms of the cemetery
findings.quote: Weathering can be described in a way that illustrates its complimentary effects on the landscape forms of the cemetery.

findings.consequent: irreversible tendency of a system toward increasing disorder
findings.quote: Entropy is the irreversible tendency of a system, including the universe, toward increasing disorder.

findings.consequent: counteract disorder by forming and building local environment
findings.quote: There is a human impulse to counteract this disorder by forming and building our local environment.

findings.consequent: demonstration of physical and psychological qualities of time's effects on built environment
findings.quote: The issue of ruins can demonstrate not just the physical but also the psychological qualities of the effects of time on our built environment.

findings.consequent: intrinsic cause of a ruin as a ruin
findings.quote: In essence, 'time is the intrinsic cause of a ruin as a ruin'(Hetzler 1988, 51).

findings.consequent: weathering (physical evidence)
findings.quote: Weathering is also an object. It is the resulting physical evidence of the process of environmental and human forces as they affect materials.

findings.consequent: weathering function
findings.quote: The manifestation of weathering is a function of the material composition of the object.

findings.consequent: primary agents of weathering
findings.quote: Climatic forces are the primary agents of weathering.

findings.consequent: deterioration of landscape architectural features
findings.quote: Deterioration because of human use is as inevitable as the elements for most landscape architectural features.

findings.consequent: important in design choices
findings.quote: Recognition of the dynamic quality of the landscape is important in the choices made in designing places.

findings.antecedent: environment, human use, design/detailing, workmanship of construction
findings.consequent: amount and nature of weathering of landscape feature
findings.quote: The environment, the human use, the design and detailing of the feature and the workmanship of the construction of the feature will all determine the amount and nature of the weathering of the feature (Simpson & Horrobin 1970, 16).

findings.antecedent: physical qualities, social conventions, cultural beliefs
findings.consequent: perception of all manifestations of objects and spaces
findings.quote: Physical qualities, social conventions and cultural beliefs all contribute to the perception of all manifestations of objects and spaces.

findings.consequent: physical and mental implications in built environment
findings.quote: The changes that weathering causes in the built environment have implications both physical and mental.

findings.antecedent: evidence of weathering in built environment
findings.consequent: varied responses (sensual, functional, abstract)
findings.quote: evidence of weathering in the built environment evokes varied responses due to the infinite mixture of sensual, functional and abstract responses by each individual.

findings.consequent: sensual-intellectual perception constitutes meaning and value
findings.quote: The landscape is therefore the setting of our lives, the sensual-intellectual perception of which constitutes meaning and value.

findings.consequent: better and reasonable guide to landscape designs
findings.quote: The recognition of human experience is a better and reasonable guide to landscape designs

findings.consequent: in the mind of the observer (not inherent in object)
findings.quote: Thayer puts forward the idea that meaning is in the mind of the observer, yet the observer acts as though meaning resides in the environment.

findings.antecedent: weathering (changing material to form patterns of wear/deterioration)
findings.consequent: addition to overall sensual experience of object/place
findings.quote: Weathering may indeed be an addition to the overall sensual experience of an object or place. By changing the material enough to form patterns of wear or other deterioration, weathering 'constructs' a finish.

findings.consequent: stimulation of senses (feel, appearance) and richness of immediate environment
findings.quote: The qualities of weathered material stimulate our senses, the feel, and appearance of an eroded landscape feature may add richness to our immediate environment.

findings.consequent: combined perception of material objects (sensual, functional, symbolic qualities + comprehension of character)
findings.quote: Materiality is the combined perception of material objects, accounting for the sensual, functional and symbolic qualities of the material and a person's comprehension of the character of the material.

findings.consequent: extra perceptual qualities to a material, changing its character
findings.quote: Weathering will add extra perceptual qualities to a material, changing a material's character because of change in physical condition or appearance.

findings.consequent: landscape weathers, providing loci for remembrance, renewal, transfiguration of culture's relationship to land
findings.quote: As time passes, this marked landscape weathers. ever subject to the contingencies of nature. Other points of view are chosen as circumstances change and new ways of marking are overlaid upon the old, producing collagic and weathered overlays[.] ...provid[ing] loci for the remembrance, renewal, and transfiguration of a culture's relationship to the land. (Corner 1991, 129)

findings.consequent: constructs finishes (rather than construction ending finishes)
findings.quote: Finishing ends construction, weathering constructs finishes.

findings.consequent: negative occurrence (detracts from ideal form/architectural idea)
findings.quote: For the majority, this weathering is a negative occurrence as it detracts from the perceived ideal of the original form or architectural idea.

findings.consequent: conflict between built and process of change
findings.quote: Weathering resides in this threshold of conflict between the built and the process of change.

findings.consequent: landscape feature successfully performs specific function
findings.quote: as long as the visual appeal of the effects of weathering does not adversely impact upon the durability, the landscape feature can successfully perform its specific function.

findings.antecedent: weathering of an object in relation to surrounding objects and environment
findings.consequent: main part of perception, bearing meaning for observer
findings.quote: it is the weathering of that object in relation to the surrounding objects and environment. The contrast or congruency of the extent of the weathering is the main part of the perception, bearing meaning for the observer.

findings.consequent: agent of unity (applies layer of wear, blending parts of place)
findings.quote: Weathering can be seen as an agent of unity in that it applies a layer of wear over the place, affecting all the parts of a place, blending them all together in their response to the environmental and human forces.

findings.consequent: impressions of dynamic balance, revealing processes of movement/action
findings.quote: Weathering can create these impressions of dynamic balance when objects are fragmented, in a sense revealing processes of movement or action.

findings.antecedent: design displaying understanding of ecological processes
findings.consequent: education for observer, visible expression of deep processes
findings.quote: A design that displays this understanding describes it and presents it for the observer's education. It is an action of giving visible expression to deep processes.

findings.consequent: expression and character of place
findings.quote: Weathering may be one of the processes and manifestations that can help to achieve this expression and character of place.

findings.antecedent: mellowed brickwork, lichen-covered stonework, silver-gray cedar boarding
findings.consequent: character qualities appreciated by people
findings.quote: Among the good examples that they find are character qualities that people seem to appreciate such as 'mellowed brickwork, lichen-covered stonework, and silver-gray cedar boarding'(Simpson & Horrobin 1970, 1).

findings.consequent: special social or cultural meaning, sensitivity to material change
findings.quote: Cemeteries have special social or cultural meaning. Consequently, they are especially sensitive to material change.

findings.antecedent: post-WWII cultural attitudes (youth focus, exclusion of death)
findings.consequent: cemeteries marginalized, less cared for by bereaved, less visited
findings.quote: In the post world war period a distinct change in cultural attitudes toward death occurred. Youth became the focus of contemporary culture, and its celebration now excludes death and the cemetery as parts of popular culture (Jackson & Vergara 1989, 118).

findings.consequent: pivotal for reconciling beliefs and emotions about death
findings.quote: The cemetery, as a place for memorial, is pivotal as a means of reconciling beliefs and emotions about death.

findings.consequent: imagery/manifestations of weathering not acceptable (in cemeteries)
findings.quote: Judging from contemporary views regarding death, there is no doubt why imagery or manifestations of weathering cannot be viewed as acceptable.

findings.consequent: desire for monument to stay immaculate in perpetuity
findings.quote: The monument represents the last remaining physical marker of the deceased. It only follows that the bereaved should desire the monument to stay in an immaculate condition in perpetuity.

findings.consequent: undesired (for bereaved), implies neglect of memory/deceased, sign of mortality
findings.quote: Weathering of the monument may be viewed as undesired as a result. ... If weathering affects the visual integrity of the cemetery monument, it is perceived as an agent of destruction. The implications of this material mortality are obvious. It denotes neglect of the monument or the memory of the deceased. It is a sign of the mortality of the bereaved.

findings.consequent: monument seen in different light (as guide to future, confers immortality)
findings.quote: The monument... confers immortality on the dead or lost, and it guides actions for the future (Jackson 1979, 93).

findings.antecedent: bereaved's perception of weathering in cemetery
findings.consequent: negative, subtractive process (takes away dignity, breeds neglect/loss)
findings.quote: In the case of the bereaved and their perception of the cemetery, character of weathering is perceived as a negative, subtractive process. It takes away a standard dignity from the monument. It breeds a feeling of neglect and loss.

findings.consequent: different meanings for weathering (not necessarily neglect/disrespect)
findings.quote: To these visitors, the process of weathering may hold different meanings, not necessarily those meanings of neglect and disrespect perceived by the bereaved.

findings.consequent: primary importance for visitor reflection and contemplation
findings.quote: The 'placeness' of the cemetery is of primary importance for the visitor who enters to reflect and contemplate.

findings.consequent: creation of atmosphere in a place, layering objects/spaces with effects of time
findings.quote: Weathering can create atmosphere in a place. It can layer the objects and spaces with the effects of time.

findings.consequent: validation of time for objects that have endured, positive cultural value
findings.quote: The patina of age is a validation of time for those objects that have endured to the present. The romantic appreciation for aging is still inherent in our culture as positive value.

findings.antecedent: weathering (perceived on impersonal basis, with mystery appeal)
findings.consequent: manifestation of decay as powerful expression to observer
findings.quote: Only when it is perceived on an impersonal basis, with the requisite mystery appeal, can the manifestation of decay be a powerful expression to the observer.

findings.consequent: interesting place to stimulate contemplation for visitors
findings.quote: The allowance of weathering in the cemetery makes it an interesting place to stimulate contemplation for visitors in a reflective state of mind.

findings.antecedent: cemetery (designed with extra intent of architectural expression)
findings.consequent: more expressive places, imagery, symbolism, metaphor communicated
findings.quote: Some cemeteries are designed with the extra intent of architectural expression. ... Imagery, symbolism and metaphor are among the additional layers of information communicated by the architects through the material forms of the cemeteries.

findings.antecedent: Igualada Cemetery design (metaphorical expression, intentional weathering)
findings.consequent: extraordinary example of expressive landscape architecture
findings.quote: This cemetery is an extraordinary example of expressive landscape architecture. It is a new cemetery near Barcelona, Spain, awarded as the winning entry in a design competition. Two architects. Enric Miralles and Carme Pinos, designed the cemetery to express a number of qualities. Among these qualities is the metaphorical expression through physical form and the intentional use of weathering as a complementary process.

findings.antecedent: Igualada Cemetery (overall form and articulation of elements)
findings.consequent: atmosphere of narrative of journey between life and death
findings.quote: The overall form and articulation of the elements creates the atmosphere of a narrative of the journey between life and death

findings.consequent: weathering as a tool of expression for death/emotional matters
findings.quote: his repeated use of the rust imagery makes the point of weathering as a tool of expression.

findings.antecedent: materials chosen for Igualada Cemetery construction
findings.consequent: affinity to change, signs of weathering interpreted as passage of time
findings.quote: The materials chosen for the construction of the cemetery demonstrate an affinity to change. Like the regular movements of the arms on a clock, the signs of weathering can be interpreted as the passage of time.

findings.consequent: heart of meaning (living place, developing, changing, welcoming visitors)
findings.quote: The transformation of materials is at the very heart of the meaning imbued in the cemetery, implying that this place for the dead is in fact a living place, which is developing and changing, and which welcomes its usage as a place to which the living can come to visit, walk and contemplate. (Zabalbeascoa 1996, 20)

findings.antecedent: weathering of cast iron (in Igualada Cemetery)
findings.consequent: cue of time's passage, visitor's place in that flow
findings.quote: The weathering of the cast iron is a cue of time's passage and the visitor's place in that flow.

findings.consequent: expression of passage of time and process of change
findings.quote: The overall cemetery expresses the passage of time and the process of change.

findings.consequent: affirmative, even restorative, vis a vis nature
findings.quote: Their attitude toward experience is poetic and intuitive: their architecture is affirmative, even restorative, vis a vis nature. (Curtis 1991,8)

findings.antecedent: trees and planting (allowed to grow and cover cemetery)
findings.consequent: softening of cemetery, merging with landscape, challenging notion of death as end
findings.quote: It was the intention of the designers that the trees and other planting would be allowed to grow and in time to cover the cemetery (Zabalbeascoa 1996, 17). This will eventually soften the cemetery, truly merging it with the surrounding landscape.

findings.consequent: encouragement of visitor reflections (life as process, not series of beginnings/endings)
findings.quote: The visual cues will encourage the reflections of the visitors. The materials provide physical and subconscious clues for the observer about the nature of time, nature and both of these contributing to the event of death/process of life.

findings.antecedent: weathered artifact (comparison present vs. past condition)
findings.consequent: perception of change, dialogue between inanimate form and thoughtful viewer
findings.quote: Perception of change arises from a person's interpretation of the weathered artifact. The comparison between the present and past condition (remembered or inferred) leads to a question: how did it arrive at its present condition? ... The reading of clues and the interpolation of events creates a dialogue between the inanimate form and the thoughtful viewer.

findings.consequent: analogy for spiritual journey of the soul, process of life and death
findings.quote: The physical representation of the spiritual journey of the soul is appropriately manifest in the Igualada Cemetery. Weathering may be a process of nature, but so is the process of life and death.

findings.antecedent: Igualada Cemetery design (physical design of site)
findings.consequent: metaphor for journey of death (descent into earth, trip back to sky)
findings.quote: The physical design of the site a metaphor for the journey of death, the descent into the earth as one enters and the trip back to the sky as one leaves (Curtis 1991, 7).

findings.antecedent: harsh/brutal character of Igualada Cemetery (weathering, angular forms)
findings.consequent: expression of emotionally charged event of death, cathartic experience for bereaved
findings.quote: The harsh and brutal character of the cemetery caused by weathering and the angular forms can also be an expression of emotionally charged event of a death (Lahuerta 1996). Such corresponding imagery can be said to create a cathartic experience for the bereaved.

findings.antecedent: Miralles's philosophy (openness to external factors, allowing change)
findings.consequent: project becomes responsive construction, stronger 'place', better fit with landscape
findings.quote: His approach to building shows an openness to external factors, factors outside and beyond the original ideas, factors which transform the project into a responsive construction that is concrete. ... By leaving the final product open to change, the project is so much stronger in its 'place', its fit into the surrounding landscape.

findings.antecedent: intentional allowance of weathering in cemetery design
findings.consequent: dialectic (merging bereaved/bystander perceptions), natural expression of landscape/nature/life process
findings.quote: This intentional allowance of weathering in the cemetery creates a dialectic. That is, it brings together the two opposing perceptions of the bereaved and the bystanders in an attempt to resolve them. What at first seems a contradiction evolves into a natural expression of landscape, nature and the analogy of the process of life.

findings.consequent: complex phenomenon (physical repercussions, perceptual impressions, material transformation, human cognition)
findings.quote: Weathering is a complex phenomenon. It encompasses both physical repercussions and perceptual impressions. It affects both material transformation and human cognition.

findings.consequent: site of conflicting views on weathering (abhorrent vs. attractive)
findings.quote: The cemetery, being an emotionally charged setting, is the site of conflicting views between the interpretation of weathering, whether it is abhorrent or attractive.

findings.consequent: source of many positive perceptual qualities of landscape, expression, sensual interest
findings.quote: Weathering can be the source of many positive perceptual qualities of the landscape. It is an integral and inevitable aspect of the environment, but it is also a source of expression and sensual interest.

findings.antecedent: physical ability of a place to gracefully weather
findings.consequent: character of a place
findings.quote: The character of a place may be a direct result of its physical ability to gracefully weather.

findings.consequent: expression of abstract ideas (passing of time, change, cycles of life)
findings.quote: Weathering can also express the nature of abstract ideas such as the passing of time, change, and the cycles of life.

findings.consequent: opportunity of rich, sensual experience
findings.quote: The weathering of an object and its surroundings can be an opportunity of rich, sensual experience. Humans need sensual environments to enrich their experiences of place.

findings.consequent: extra stimuli for the senses
findings.quote: Weathering of landscape features offers some extra stimuli for the senses.

findings.antecedent: ragged outline, rough surface, contrasting colors, overgrown stones, wind sounds (of ruins)
findings.consequent: sense impressions, part of mental lives
findings.quote: Their ragged outline and rough surface were palpably irregular. They displayed contrasting colors since their old stones were overgrown with ivy and variegated wall flowers; nor did they fail to strike the ear with the moaning of the wind.. (Baridon 1985,93)

findings.consequent: impoverished experience in the world
findings.quote: The loss of this sensual environment has been observed to have impoverished our experience in the world.

findings.antecedent: meaninglessness of environment, incomprehensibility to senses
findings.consequent: irrational fear in cities, loss of primary causality in sensory experience
findings.quote: The irrational fear in our cities grows out of the meaninglessness of the environment to our reason and its incomprehensibility to our senses. We are losing the primary causality in our sensory experience of the world. (Pallasmaa 1994, 25)

findings.consequent: important for quality of landscapes, interest in places
findings.quote: Natural processes that generate and deliver these sensual stimuli are important to the quality of landscapes. They provide the interest in places that humans crave.

findings.consequent: agent for communication of more than sensory interest, vehicle for ideas, tool of expression
findings.quote: Weathering is an agent for the communication of more than sensory interest. It can be the vehicle for ideas as well, a tool of expression.

findings.antecedent: Vietnam memorial (simple wall, incised in earth)
findings.consequent: speaks to visitor on many levels of perceptual experience (physical, psychological), expresses discomforting symbolism
findings.quote: The power of this simple wall lies in the complexity of its message, its ambiguous form and context of its location. This wall, incised in the earth speaks to the visitor on many levels of perceptual experience, physically and psychologically. It is exceptional because it is different from the majority of war monuments that are erect and proud. It expresses potentially discomforting symbolism with its subtle, earthbound composition, expressing potential misgivings about that war effort.

findings.consequent: integral and valuable aspect of built environment
findings.quote: Acceptance and inclusion of weathering can be an integral and valuable aspect of our built environment.

findings.consequent: communication to observer if interpreted as planned circumstance
findings.quote: If weathering is used as a metaphorical expression, it may only communicate to the observer if it is interpreted as a planned circumstance.

findings.consequent: less intimidating, more acceptable, adds to atmosphere on subconscious level
findings.quote: A subtle expression can be less intimidating and hopefully more acceptable since it is not forcing the judgment of the observer. It may simply add to the atmosphere of the place, leaving impressions on a subconscious level.

findings.antecedent: person seeing broken/changed object (memory of past condition)
findings.consequent: interpretation of cause, reaction
findings.quote: When a person sees something that is broken, or not in the condition that it once was, that person can interpret what caused the change. ... Memory allows someone to see an object and remember its past condition and compare that image that is present. The comparison between the different conditions is an act of interpretation that leads to a reaction.

findings.consequent: representation of change without compromising integrity/function of objects
findings.quote: The manifestations [of weathering at Igualada] truly represent the process of change but they do not compromise the integrity of the objects, nor do they hinder their functions.

findings.consequent: opportunities for objects to compliment/unify with surroundings
findings.quote: Weathering is consistent with all the elements. They can be perceived as intentional effects, desired as meaningful, not accidental. The opportunities of weathering are centered on the ability of an object to compliment, and to be unified with, its surroundings.

findings.antecedent: weathering (as part of natural processes of change)
findings.consequent: part of how people relate to environment, understand world
findings.quote: Weathering is part of the natural processes of change, yet it is also a part of how people relate to their environment, how they understand their world.

findings.consequent: replacement of older cemeteries as desired burial places
findings.quote: Cemeteries that do not exhibit any signs of weathering are replacing older cemeteries as desired places for the interment of the dead.

findings.consequent: factor in public desires for cemeteries
findings.quote: The control over the processes of nature is a factor in these desires by the public.

findings.antecedent: weathering (perceived as unnecessary, visually distressing, preventable)
findings.consequent: unacceptable
findings.quote: If weathering is perceived as unnecessary, visually distressing or preventable, it may be unacceptable.

findings.antecedent: North American context (urban decay, derelict land)
findings.consequent: weathering as messenger of bad news, embodiment of guilt/anger/despair
findings.quote: North America does not share the same respect for the old and dilapidated that Europeans might for their aged buildings and landscapes. Here, weathering is the messenger of bad news, standing as witnesses to a past that still stirring with persistent emotions (Vergara 1994, 19).

findings.consequent: source of positive qualities in cemeteries/landscapes, expression, sensual interest
findings.quote: weathering can be the source of many positive qualities of cemeteries and other landscapes. It is an integral and inevitable aspect of the environment, but it is also a source of expression and sensual interest.

findings.consequent: representation of natural forces, inevitable cycles of life and nature
findings.quote: weathered objects and spaces represent the natural forces that cause the change as well as the inevitable cycles of life and nature.

findings.consequent: tolerate weathering in an elegant fashion
findings.quote: materials that have a consistent composition throughout its form can tolerate weathering in an elegant fashion.

findings.consequent: exploitation of patinization of objects and spaces
findings.quote: In order to exploit the patinization of objects and spaces a degree of control must be relinquished.

findings.antecedent: objects/spaces maintain integrity of form and function
findings.consequent: any weathering perceived as acceptable ('graceful weathering')
findings.quote: Generally, as long as the objects and spaces maintain an integrity of form and function, any weathering can still within the parameters of what is perceived as acceptable.

findings.antecedent: harsh or violent manifestations of weathering (destruction of form, loss of visual integrity/function)
findings.consequent: distress
findings.quote: Harsh or violent manifestations of weathering can be distressing. These include destruction of form and loss of the visual integrity of and object's function.

findings.consequent: opportunities for expression in form and place
findings.quote: Being flexible in the design process means planning for and accepting change in the landscape. An understanding of weathering applied to the choice of materials that will change allows the opportunities for expression in form and place.

findings.antecedent: industrial, materialistic view of architecture and nature
findings.consequent: fragmented experience, separation from natural processes, not enriching
findings.quote: Our industrial, materialistic view of architecture and nature is fragmented because we try to freeze the fluid actions of the environment in discrete frames. ... This approach separates human life from the harmonious processes of nature. (Lawlor 1995, 204)

findings.consequent: reminder of natural processes, mortality, cycle of life
findings.quote: Maybe the consideration of weathering evokes different feelings in each person, but it does serve as a reminder of natural processes. It reminds a person about the mortality of all things in the cycle of life.

findings.consequent: richness of perceptual environment
findings.quote: One is the identification of graceful weathering and how this adds to the richness of the perceptual environment.

findings.consequent: meaningful design expressing ecology and change
findings.quote: By including an understanding of weathering in the design process, a meaningful design that expresses notions of ecology and change can be achieved.

findings.antecedent: materials that accept and are graced by weathering
findings.consequent: visually appealing and mentally stimulating landscape
findings.quote: Weathering can be a visually appealing and mentally stimulating part of the landscape if the materials accept, and are graced by, this process of change.

findings.antecedent: designer understanding weathering as complex system
findings.consequent: abandonment of deterministic approach to controlling landscape outcome
findings.quote: If a designer understands weathering as a complex system of physical behavior and forces, he/she must abandon the deterministic approach to controlling the total outcome of a constructed landscape.

findings.antecedent: design process accounting for weathering (informed material choice/positioning)
findings.consequent: expression of ideas, emotions, metaphors
findings.quote: All the expressions previously described are possible if the process of weathering is accounted in an informed design process, choosing and positioning materials in interesting and knowledgeable ways.

findings.antecedent: allowance for weathering effects (even if not explicit design parameter)
findings.consequent: space gracefully merges with surrounding landscape, takes on local climate characteristics
findings.quote: Even if the weathering is not included explicitly as a design parameter, the allowance for its wearing effects can eventually change a space so that it gracefully merges with its surrounding landscape, taking on the adjacent characteristics that the local climate has already affected.

findings.antecedent: understanding of weathering, its manifestations, human perceptions
findings.consequent: better design of landscape features
findings.quote: Understanding the process of weathering, its manifestations and the perceptions of humans in various contexts can lead to better design of landscape features.

findings.antecedent: material and real qualities of designed features
findings.consequent: speak to perceptual being within each person
findings.quote: The material and real qualities of our designed features should speak to the perceptual being within each of person.

findings.consequent: landscapes harmonious with natural processes, maintaining function/form integrity, accessible to users
findings.quote: The insights about graceful weathering and flexible design can create landscapes harmonious with natural processes while still maintaining an integrity of function and form. These places may be congruent with the forces of weathering while remaining accessible to the human users.

findings.consequent: valuable, explicit part of design process
findings.quote: Weathering can be a valuable, explicit part of this process of design.

findings.consequent: important part of relationship with built environment, means of communication/provocation
findings.quote: The expression designed into the landscapes that we build is an important part of our relationship with the built environment. It is a means of communication or provocation, transmitting stimuli to the observers of the landscape.

findings.consequent: important aspect of built environment, clue to passage of time/change, honest material transformation
findings.quote: Weathering is one range of natural processes in the landscape. It only follows that the expression of weathering is an important aspect of our built environment and a clue to the passage of time and change in the world. It can express honest material transformation, revealing change literally to the observer.

limitations: The study is a descriptive practicum based on literature review and a case study, not empirical data collection on human responses (page 9).
Perceptions of weathering are 'read in the criticism of others' rather than directly observed or measured from visitors (page 9).
The case study of Igualada Cemetery is a 'foreign context compared to Canadian cemeteries and its exact way of expression cannot be copied' (page 66).
Not all people have the patience for the expression of weathering (page 74).
There is a dilemma for the designer on how to design for both the bereaved and the bystander, whose perceptions of weathering conflict (page 55).
minimum_safe_summary: This practicum investigates the dichotomy of weathering in cemeteries, exploring how its physical manifestations are perceived differently by bereaved visitors (who often view it as neglect and a sign of mortality) and bystanders (who may appreciate it as an expression of time, history, and natural cycles). Through a literature review and a case study of Igualada Cemetery, the study argues that weathering can be a valuable, expressive element in landscape architectural design, communicating abstract ideas like life, death, and change, and enriching the sensual and psychological experience of a place. The paper concludes with insights for designers to embrace graceful weathering and flexible design strategies, acknowledging the inevitable process of material transformation. Limitations include the theoretical nature of the study, relying on interpretations from literature rather than direct empirical data on visitor perceptions, and the cultural specificity of the case study.
